stem: A client with multiple sclerosis develops new visual disturbance and numbness that persist for two days. What is the nurse's best interpretation?

options.A: The symptoms are a pseudo-relapse because any new neurologic symptom lasting more than 24 hours is caused by heat, stress, fever, or infection.
options.B: The symptoms are routine daily fluctuation and do not require assessment when they persist for two days.
options.C: The findings may represent an MS relapse and warrant prompt evaluation, including assessment for infection, fever, heat, stress, or another pseudo-relapse trigger.
options.D: The symptoms establish permanent disease progression because an MS relapse cannot cause new visual or sensory findings.

rationale: Current U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs multiple-sclerosis guidance describes a relapse as new or worsening neurologic symptoms lasting more than 24 hours that reflect new inflammatory activity and are not better explained by infection, fever, heat, stress, or another pseudo-relapse trigger. Visual and sensory symptoms can occur with MS relapses. New symptoms persisting for two days therefore warrant prompt evaluation by the MS care team, including assessment for pseudo-relapse triggers and other causes; the vignette alone does not establish a definite relapse. Therefore C is correct. A incorrectly labels all prolonged symptoms as pseudo-relapse, B dismisses symptoms that require assessment, and D incorrectly equates a possible relapse with permanent progression.
educational_objective: Recognize new or worsening neurologic symptoms lasting more than 24 hours in multiple sclerosis as possible relapse requiring evaluation while first assessing for infection, fever, heat, stress, or other pseudo-relapse triggers.
source_organization: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs — Multiple Sclerosis Centers of Excellence
source_document_title: Relapse Management for Multiple Sclerosis; What is Multiple Sclerosis?
source_version_date: Current VA MS guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Relapse Management for Multiple Sclerosis: relapse involves new/worsening MS symptoms lasting >24 hours; contact MS provider for new/worsening symptoms; evaluate for infection and other triggers; pseudo-relapses can occur with infection, stress, and heat. What is MS?: relapse is major worsening of old symptoms or new symptoms lasting at least 24 hours and not caused by infection, fever, or stress.
source_claim_supported: New visual or sensory neurologic symptoms persisting more than 24 hours in a person with MS may represent relapse and warrant prompt evaluation, but infection, fever, heat, stress and other pseudo-relapse triggers should be assessed before concluding a true relapse.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: recognize new or worsening neurologic alterations, distinguish complications from transient triggers, and intervene appropriately for acute changes in chronic neurologic disease.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — multiple-sclerosis relapse versus pseudo-relapse

source_original.stem: A client with multiple sclerosis develops new visual disturbance and numbness that persist for two days. What is the nurse's best interpretation?

options.A: The symptoms are a pseudo-relapse because any new neurologic symptom lasting more than 24 hours is caused by heat or infection.
options.B: The symptoms are routine daily fluctuation and do not require assessment when they persist for two days.
options.C: The findings may represent an MS relapse and warrant evaluation, including assessment for infection, fever, heat, or another pseudo-relapse trigger.
options.D: The symptoms establish permanent disease progression because an MS relapse cannot cause new visual or sensory findings.

source_original.rationale: A true MS relapse is characterized by new or worsening neurologic symptoms lasting more than 24 hours and not explained by infection, fever, or another pseudo-relapse trigger. New persistent visual and sensory symptoms therefore warrant prompt assessment by the MS care team.
source_original.source_detail: Definition of MS relapse and recommendation to contact the MS provider for new or worsening symptoms lasting more than 24 hours Source has no separate formal version identifier in the cited page metadata; live currentness and applicability rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the relapse-versus-pseudo-relapse construct and key C, added stress to the trigger assessment, preserved the nondefinitive 'may represent' wording, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a defined relapse-recognition rule plus exclusion of common pseudo-relapse triggers.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current VA Multiple Sclerosis Centers of Excellence guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: VA MS relapse and disease-information pages live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: VA Relapse Management for Multiple Sclerosis and What is Multiple Sclerosis? relapse definitions and trigger assessment
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item identifies a possible relapse requiring evaluation rather than diagnosing relapse solely from duration; it explicitly preserves assessment for infection, fever, heat, stress, and other pseudo-relapse triggers.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because symptoms lasting >24 hours are not automatically pseudo-relapse and require assessment for true relapse and triggers.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because new persistent neurologic symptoms for two days warrant MS-team assessment.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because relapses can cause new visual/sensory symptoms and do not by themselves establish permanent disease progression.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C preserves both possibilities—true relapse versus pseudo-relapse trigger—while directing appropriate evaluation.
audit_findings.cueing: All options interpret the same neurologic change and duration; the key depends on relapse criteria and trigger exclusion.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — neurologic change recognition and complication assessment.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current VA relapse-management guidance, relapse definition, pseudo-relapse triggers, visual/sensory symptom relevance, all options, rationale, objective, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN mapping. C remained uniquely correct.
